speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Hey, this is Carlos, CEO at Product School and your host on The Product Podcast. My guest today is Amjad Masad, CEO of Replit. Ten years in, and he says the first eight were just finding product-market fit. Then they shipped the agent, did 100x revenue in a year, and now they're at 50 million users and a $9 billion valuation, chasing a billion in revenue. Over 75% of those users are not engineers. And he corrects me early on: nobody in AI has recurring revenue, it's run-rate revenue. Here are the things we'll cover: why he says chat was never the thing, code is; not knowing how to code is now an advantage; his prompts have gotten lazier on purpose; the self-driving company, and why he thinks it's mid next year; and frontier performance at 40% of the cost through model routing. Let's get into it. [Sponsor]  AI helps us generate ideas, draft plans, and spin up work in minutes. But faster doesn't necessarily mean better. When everyone has their own AI tools, their own outputs, and their own context, you get fragmentation: fractured version control, scattered review processes, decisions happening in parallel, not in concert. Rebuilding context between people and platforms costs you time and momentum. That's where Mural comes in. Mural gives teams a shared visual canvas to bring work together. You can generate structured starting points right on the canvas instead of moving outputs between tools, keep all of your context in one place, and compatible AI agents can contribute alongside the team, bringing in context from the tools they already know. The future of work is still human. Learn more at mural.co. Ten Years In, Eight Spent Finding Product-Market Fit

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Amjad, welcome to The Product Podcast.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Thanks for having me. My nine-year-old son couldn't be here, but he asked me to say thank you, because he's been vibe coding some video games on Replit.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: That's awesome.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Video games have gotten so good with AI, it's crazy. I was just at a booth, one of our sales engineers is always making video games with Replit, and he showed me a FIFA that he made. I'm like, this is better than the FIFA I played growing up, and it was one prompt.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Wow. But not everything was rainbows and sunshine. You've been grinding for ten years, and the first eight were kind of the beginning of finding product-market fit. So what's been happening? What do you think was that pivotal moment where you felt like you'd already hit product-market fit?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: In the history of startups, we've always had this idea that you spend two years in seed, two years in Series A, you get product-market fit, and you scale from there. But I think that was only a SaaS-era phenomenon. If you look at older businesses, it takes about five, six, seven, eight years to build something meaningful. Even recently, when you look at businesses like Notion or Figma, or some of our peers from that era, it took them a while to get there. So I've had the patience, because I felt like we were riding on certain trends that were going to become more and more important in the future. One was cloud, two was AI, three was mobile, and four was collaboration and the future of work. So I've always had conviction. Obviously there are times when there's a lot of self-doubt, but when we were working on Replit Agent, we kind of knew it was the future. It was a rough time for the company. We had just done a layoff, because we were spending a lot of money and not making any. But the group of people, about 30 of us, working on Replit Agent, which is really the first coding agent on the market, there were no examples of coding agents at the time, the moment we started seeing it work internally, we just had tremendous conviction in it. Still, we didn't know we were going to get 100x revenue in a year. No one predicts that. It's really hard to predict. But we knew it was the future. Run-Rate Revenue, Not ARR

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So a few years forward, now you're at over 50 million users, a $9 billion valuation, and you're aiming for $1 billion in annual recurring revenue by the end of this year. How is that going?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: By the way, no one in AI has annual recurring revenue, so we need to get used to seeing run-rate revenue. But yeah, things are going well. A few things are interesting. Enterprise adoption of AI has really advanced this year. If you look at the last few years, since GPT-3, enterprises were not really using AI. ChatGPT started to change that, and then Microsoft Copilot. But if you look at most enterprises today, they just use chat. Most people here who work at large companies, if you're not an engineer, engineers are typically on the cutting edge, but if you're not an engineer, you just get access to a chat and maybe some RAG system. But now this year, we're starting to see big banks sign up to Replit, big financial institutions, Visa, Amex, some of our customers, governments. The US government is a customer. So we're finally starting to see how AI could transform work and how we do work, because I don't think chat really has a big impact. There was this big question: "we're investing so much in AI, we're not seeing impact." I don't think chat is the thing. I really think ultimately code is the thing. The idea that everyone can make software, can create code, and can work with agents, and most agents are coding agents essentially, to get their work done, that's quite transformative for the economy. We're in the early innings of that, but the compounding nature of it is quite astounding. Why Not Knowing How to Code Is an Advantage

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to learn more about it, because it seems like over 75% of your users are non-engineers. And I hear you say that not knowing how to code can actually give you an advantage.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: I think people who have been coding with AI for a while are also at a disadvantage, because the most recent generations of AI models, the frontier ones, are actually better with very simple prompts. My prompts have gotten lazier over time. I use fewer skill files. Models are getting more and more capable, so the more you try to micromanage them, the worse they are. There's this wisdom in Silicon Valley that micromanagement is not great, which is true: if you have a talented engineer, you shouldn't be micromanaging them. But most engineers' instinct is to micromanage the AI. Whereas someone who doesn't have that instinct might actually get better results. You're starting to see that.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I saw that with Replit Agent. You're able to spawn multiple sub-agents. The next thought that comes to that is, how do you orchestrate or oversee, I don't want to say micromanage, but make sure you at least have a good sense of what's going on as a human user?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: So the UI needs to give you that. With parallel agents, we have a thread for each one of them. You can dig into each thread of work and see what's going on. Also, agents come back with questions, and we have the mobile app. If you install it, it'll send you a message, like, "hey, I'm going to go over budget," or "I'm going to use this new package," or "I'm going to do this refactor." So you have that oversight. And the agent kind of learns your pattern of usage. If you're someone who is totally hands-off, the agent learns that. But if you're an engineer who is micromanaging the AI and that's what you prefer, more power to you, and it'll adapt to that. The Self-Driving Company

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So you recently coined this term, the self-driving company. How can companies learn to learn?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: There's a compounding nature of learning to learn, very much like everything we generate can go back into context. The problem now with most companies is that most people are using Claude or ChatGPT on the desktop, and that is actually not feeding back into context. At Replit, most of our AI usage happens in Slack, a lot of it in public channels. So everything is self-referential. We write documents, they go back into the context, and so collaboration becomes very important. We spend a lot of time figuring out how to do collaboration with AI on Replit, like having multiple people in the same project. None of the big labs are focused on that, but I think that's a mistake. It's more important right now to approach building companies more collaboratively and doing work more collaboratively, because we're going to have less work on our plate to go do as individual contributors. And where new ideas emerge happens from brainstorming, from building on each other's ideas. You almost want to approach building a company like an open-source community, where things might be a little chaotic and there's no centralized leader, but everyone's building on top of each other's things, everyone's learning from one another. I think that's the future of how companies work. As companies become more autonomous, when a lot of the engineering is autonomous, when the support is autonomous, when a lot of the operations are autonomous, you have to ask, what is the role of the human? Ultimately, I think it is knowing what the customer wants. Figuring out what's the best thing to build, figuring out the major decisions, setting the destination, and then trusting the self-driving autonomy of the company to do it. Slack as an Operating System, and What Comes Next

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: The unlock for me was being able to start using it within Slack. I see you also have a similar integration with Claude Code. So I'm curious how you're thinking about those external user interfaces as a way to enhance collaboration.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: I think we're all trying to discover what that looks like. I don't think anyone has figured out the best kind of user interface. I think "operating system" is the right question. We're all using Slack as an operating system in some ways for companies, but it is not a good one. It's basically a dumping ground for all text, and it's become very hard for the human user to absorb everything, which is why we're having to rely on agents more and more to summarize the communication, to summarize what's happening. You might want, at some point, human-only interfaces, because a lot of the stuff agents generate is like chains of thought that you might not want to worry about. So there's a question of legibility here, but I think it's a very open question, and it's one of the biggest startup opportunities today: figuring out what that is. Increasing Output Without Sacrificing Quality

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: For the technical user, for the engineer, one of the things I noticed is that you published on your blog that you were able to increase your code output without sacrificing quality and other traditional trade-offs you'd expect from just putting more gas into the fire. So how are you able to combine that, to increase productivity and throughput without making the quality suffer?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Early on, when the whole vibe-coding thing was happening, Replit was probably the only player that was compute maximalist. We were always trying to generate the best software, the most secure, and we built a lot of the things you can string together in the market. We have built-in code review, we have a built-in security agent, and it made it a little more expensive, a little slower, but you can trust the results more. Now internally at Replit, we all use that to build Replit itself. So internally, we're a lot more comfortable than most companies opening pull requests to designers, even to salespeople. The reason a lot of companies might not want to open that up is because there's still a safety issue, still a code-quality issue. But if you have really good systems and guardrails, I think most companies would want to open up their GitHub repos to non-engineers.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: But are those guardrails and systems created by default, or do companies need to set up something to make sure the quality is there?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Bigger companies need to do that. Smaller companies, it's more by default. With bigger companies, we started doing, and everyone's doing it now, the FDE model, where we go in, we figure out the requirements, and we work with them to encode their guidelines and style guides. In many cases, at banks and big financial institutions, there's a lot of compliance and regulatory issues, and those are very tough. This is a big reason, as a lot of people who work at these companies would know, why AI has not seen tremendous adoption. There are so many ways things can go wrong. So they require a little bit more handholding.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: You also have about 85% Fortune 500 adoption.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Yeah, in terms of usage. In terms of enterprise contracts, it's significantly less than that, but it's catching up. Frontier Performance at 40% of the Cost

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: The other big piece, I think, is the model routing. Some enterprises will have their own criteria for what the options are for their teams. How do you go about that type of routing?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: We promise our customers that we'll get them the best token for the cheapest price for any given task. Because we've accumulated a lot of data on usage over the past three or four years, we train models that can figure out not just model size, but also reasoning effort and so on. We've published benchmarks on our website showing that we can get frontier performance at 40% of the cost, pretty consistently. So when you buy Replit, in most cases, again, there are big enterprises and governments that have certain restrictions, but in most cases we want the customer to trust us with the model selection. We have zero-data-retention contracts with all the different providers. If we have that freedom, we're always going to be at frontier performance, but also significantly cheaper. Collaborating With the Labs While Competing With Them

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I think that's a market-dynamic situation where you're collaborating with OpenAI and Anthropic, and at the same time you could be considered a competitor. So how do you navigate that dichotomy?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: We've always had this issue. We've been a Google Cloud customer for a long time, and they've been trying to compete with us ever since I remember. They had an online IDE, and they had something before that, and they're probably all dead now. Now they have Google Studio. It never really bothered me. The way I view these big companies is that there are two or three things they can't lose on, and then they're going to do a hundred or a thousand things that are less important to them. Initially, when everyone was adding vibe coding to their platforms, a lot of investors were really worried about us. I kept saying that we just do this one thing, which is we're a one-stop shop for creating software, and the depth of the platform is very important. For the consumer use cases, anyone can make any sort of website anywhere, you can ask any agent to make that. But if you want to build a business on Replit, if you want to operate a business, I think we're still the best at that, because we provide all the infrastructure, the security guarantees, compliance, privacy, and so on. If you build a website on Codex or whatever, they send it to Cloudflare, some external provider, to host it for you. With us, it's all one thing. So the agent has access to the entire environment, development and production. We also have better control, because you only trust one player, as opposed to trusting three or four different providers.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Totally. I think as the model commoditizes, the value gets pushed upstream, and the application layer has more differentiation. Plus, you don't have to do the heavy investment in building the infrastructure.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: That's the main thing. Our power users tend to be either entrepreneurs who are building multi-million-dollar businesses, many times solo, or corporate employees doing amazing things with Replit. The common thing between these two groups is that they don't want to manage infra.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Someone told me the difference between micromanagement and attention to detail is how much agency you give to the person on the other end.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Yeah. When the Self-Driving Company Arrives

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: So going back to the self-driving company, I think that's a fascinating concept that still feels futuristic. How far do you think we are from mainstream adoption, where companies can confidently say, okay, we have some automated feedback loops here?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: I would say mid next year, companies will be comfortably running agents doing real work. Right now, most agents happen on employees' laptops. Very few companies, perhaps outside of tech, are using agents to do real workflows. So I think mid next year, it'll feel like you really have digital coworkers.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: In the last few weeks, we're also starting to see massive adoption of these AI assistants. How does that super cycle impact your business?

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: It's good in that more people knowing the power of these tools will demand their companies have them, or bring some of these tools to their companies. It's challenging in that I don't think consumer vibe coding is a viable market anymore. It's something we've made some money on, but from the start I knew that was going to happen. That's why I always thought we should monetize enterprise and businesses and not really monetize consumer. So now we have a free plan: you subscribe for $20 and you can just code forever, we have an effectively unlimited plan now. But I think it's all good. The more people understand how impactful these tools can be in their lives or their work, the faster adoption will happen, and that's good for our business.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: I want to leave it here. It would be awesome if, one year from now, six months from now, we're sitting next to each other and we say, "remember what you said?"

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Yes. There's so much to the adoption of this self-driving company. I think it's one of the best times to be alive. There's a lot of things to build. A lot of people are trying to convince you that there's no reason to create startups or businesses anymore. There's tremendous opportunity, and at least for the next two years, it's an amazing time.

speaker: Carlos González de Villaumbrosia
text: Thank you.

speaker: Amjad Masad
text: Of course.
